We extend 6 the same generator formula to every ρ ∈(0, 1) using the compact closed convex hull. The proof combines 12 the classical Christoffel endpoint transition with a quotient-shift convex decomposition and an 13 explicit rational support separator. 14 The assignment is Hausdorff-continuous at every irrational parameter. 1 Introduction 26

Perrot, Boro´nski and Clark [13] associate to each irrational parameter ρ ∈(0, 1) an explicit symmetric, 27 nonpolygonal rotation set Kρ. We determine the exact one-sided trace and continuity law of the 28 defining convex-hull formula. Under the closed-hull convention fixed below, the same formula is 29 meaningful at rational parameters as well. For every reduced rational r = p/q, its exact value is the 30 left Hausdorff trace, while the right trace is a larger finite rational polygon: 31

At a fixed truncation level, the finite nonaxial 1 generator set is locally constant away from rational walls of bounded denominator; a uniform tail 2 estimate controls all omitted indices. The support certificate does more than prove strictness: it gives universal Hausdorff and area lower 1 bounds proportional to q−3 and q−4, respectively. These bounds are not claimed to be sharp; see 2 Remark 5.5. The mechanism separates the classical symbolic input from the new convex geometry. 3 A single Christoffel endpoint changes the rational residue pattern, an exact quotient-shift identity 4 collapses the infinite family to finitely many residue generators and a common axial diamond, and a 5 rational support functional exposes the newly admitted generator beyond the lower trace. 6 The rational jumps form only one half of the parameter law. At every irrational parameter the 7 assignment is Hausdorff-continuous, and its upper modulus is governed by Diophantine separation 8 from rational walls of bounded denominator. The canonical formula is left-continuous with right 9 limits and is continuous exactly at the irrationals. Liouville approximation, combined with the 10 quantitative jump bound, rules out every positive pointwise H¨older exponent at a Liouville parameter. 11 The reciprocal roundness jumps are not summable, forcing infinite total variation on every interval 12 adjacent to zero; variation on intervals bounded away from zero remains open. 13 Continued fractions reveal a second arithmetic layer. Only residues on the active ceiling envelope 14 can contribute exposed trace generators. Identifying that envelope with the interior hull of a clean 15 lattice parallelogram reduces the raw quadratic residue search to O((log q)2) candidate pairs. For 16 Fibonacci convergents this structure becomes recursive: successive traces are obtained by adjoining 17 one dihedral orbit, and the normalized jumps obey an exact parity-dependent cubic scaling law. 18 This continued-fraction layer uses the cited lattice-hull theorem; the trace, strictness and regularity 19 results do not. 20 Each rational trace polygon is individually realizable as a rotation set of a torus homeomorphism, 21 but the present results do not construct a continuous family of realizing systems. They also do not 22 decide the broader question whether a Euclidean disk can occur as a torus rotation set. S7. Discussion and scope

The main conclusion is an information statement about spectral compression, not merely a fluctuation formula. At the Gaussian base point, the complete spectrum retains a rank-one standardized non-Gaussian tangent in the growing matrix limit, and the retained fourthcumulant information is exhausted by two low-order trace coordinates. The likelihood theorem then shows that this score governs the actual local experiment, including testing risk and asymptotic sufficiency. The result is deliberately local. The positive finite-Hermite path supplies a regular neighborhood on which the complete spectral likelihood is controlled uniformly in dimension. The theorem does not claim global sufficiency of two traces, universality for all distributions with a common fourth moment, or a fixed-alternative likelihood limit. Covariance robustness is first-order at the white Gaussian base point, and the current argument does not yet cover colored population covariance, dependent entries, or an infinite-Hermite perturbation without an additional uniform tail condition.

The separation between matrix size and independent replication is therefore substantive. A larger single spectrum stabilizes an order-one kurtosis channel; it does not create diverging local information. Replication adds independent copies of that channel and produces the Gaussian shift experiment. The Supplementary Material records higher-cumulant replication scales, singular odd-direction recovery, the GOE comparison, and additional analytic derivatives, but these are not needed for the central result.

Colored covariance

A non-scalar population covariance breaks the left orthogonal symmetry that forces the white model onto a one-dimensional standardized entry-law tangent. The retained score may then couple different Hermite coordinates to different parts of the population spectrum. Three regimes should be distinguished. First, if a structured Σ is known, one can ask for the exact entry-law score conditional on its sample spectrum. The central question is therefore whether the white rank-one geometry becomes a finite-rank system indexed by moments of Σ, or a genuinely infinite-rank geometry indexed by its full spectral law. This is the most important step toward covariance sensing, heteroscedastic data, and realistic applications.

S13.5. Broader conceptual programs

Information-valued freeness

Second-order freeness describes Gaussian and Wishart trace fluctuations [4, 12], but fluctuation covariance alone does not define a statistical tangent, a likelihood, or a Fisher metric. A possible long-term framework would enrich second-order free probability with a Fisher geometry on perturbations of the entry law. At minimum, such a theory should:

1. recover the exact hierarchy (10) and constants 𝑐𝑟without entrywise Haar pairings; 2. recover the mean and variance likelihood channels in Chebyshev coordinates; and 3. provide composition rules for the retained information under sums and products of independent ensembles.

The first falsifiable target is the Wishart hierarchy itself. Products of independent ensembles would then provide a setting where an abstract composition theory offers a genuine advantage over direct invariant calculation.

An intrinsic singular information geometry

The skewness example shows that when the observation map annihilates a first-order tangent, second-order inference can depend on arbitrary path curvature. This issue is not specific to random matrices. A broader theory should define intrinsic higher-order information on a quotient that removes visible lower-order curvature, specify the correct boundary local scales, and supply convolution or optimality bounds for singular experiments. Random matrix spectra provide a concrete test case because the reflection quotient is exact and the induced even-chaos components can be calculated explicitly.

Lemma S8.6 and Proposition S8.9 establish a nonzero complex 𝐿2 neighborhood uniform over 𝑝, 𝑛, which is the key input for simultaneous fourth-cumulant LAN. The present constants are deliberately conservative: capacity comparison loses at most 𝑒2𝑘at exterior level 𝑘, the reverse-Hardy argument reduces the usable determinant radius, and the circular Fourier density is kept comfortably inside its positivity region. Sharpening these steps could identify the maximal analytic neighborhood, improve finite-𝜂likelihood and total-variation bounds, and clarify where the local approximation actually fails. Weingarten calculus [13] may be useful for exact low-order corrections, even though the determinant-capacity argument is better suited to all-order summability.

S13.7. Closing perspective

The paper identifies the exact finite-dimensional Fisher geometry of non-Gaussian entry perturbations after covariance-spectrum compression. At the white Gaussian point, odd directions are removed exactly, higher even cumulants are progressively suppressed, and kurtosis is the unique standardized first-order direction retaining order-one information. One spectrum reaches a bounded information ceiling, whereas independent replication accumulates the surviving signal and produces a Gaussian shift. The entire local kurtosis experiment is then captured by an explicit aggregate of two trace power sums. The open problems above test the universality of that picture. They ask what remains when rotational symmetry is broken, invisible tangents are studied at second order, the number of active cumulants grows, or the matrix symmetry class changes. In each case the guiding question is the same:

Which distributional directions survive spectral compression, and at what replication cost?

The computational results in this paper have a deliberately limited role. They test algebraic constants, finite-sample cross-triggering, and consequences of the score-mean waveform theorem. Hardware protocols and application-development material are therefore excluded from this theory-first manuscript and retained as a separate future project.

# Positive Reflection Symmetrizers: Random Walks and an Abel–Young Character of Ordered Trees

Surya Tallavarjulaa,∗, Seyed Ali Rastegarb

aDepartment of Physics, University of California, Berkeley, CA, 94720, USA bDepartment of Mathematics, University of California, Berkeley, CA, 94720, USA

## Abstract

Let W be a finite well-generated complex reflection group. We introduce an ordered reflection symmetrizer obtained by averaging products of cyclic Reynolds projectors over rank-sized reflection generating sets, and prove that it is central and positive semidefinite in every unitary representation via a recursion over codimension-one parabolic subgroups. In type A, the normalized symmetrizer is a random walk generated by independently activating edges of a uniformly edge-ordered Cayley tree. We determine its exact class law and an exact convex-mixture representation by conjugacy-averaged uniform measures on Young subgroups; the multiplicities form a nonnegative integral Young permutation character. Abel real-rootedness and normalized Schur monotonicity order the complete Specht spectrum by dominance and give the exact spectral gap. We also prove total-variation cutoff at log k/(log 2 + 1/2). For G(m, 1, 2), we obtain an exact subgroup-idempotent formula and normalized spectrum {0, 1/4, 1}.

Keywords: complex reflection groups, positive semidefinite group-algebra elements, random walks, ordered trees, Abel polynomials, Young permutation characters 2020 MSC: 05E10, 20F55, 05E05, 20C30, 05E18, 05C05

## 1. Introduction

Products of orthogonal projectors are usually neither self-adjoint nor positive. This paper studies a setting in which a highly noncommutative sum of such products nevertheless becomes a positive central operator. Given a finite well-generated complex reflection group, choose an ordered minimal reflection generating set, average independently over the cyclic subgroup of each reflection, multiply in the chosen order, and then sum over all choices. The resulting group-algebra element is positive semidefinite in every unitary representation. Its recursive decomposition is canonically indexed by the codimension-one parabolic subgroups. The normalization also gives the construction an operational meaning. It is a probability measure obtained by first choosing a uniform ordered good generating set and then choosing a uniform power of each reflection. Thus the same theorem produces a conjugation-invariant Markov chain with no negative eigenvalues. This places the operator in the broad representation-theoretic tradition of random walks on finite groups [1], while the proof mechanism is specific to reflection-generating prefixes. For the symmetric group, the walk has a concrete tree sampler. Choose a uniform labeled tree, order its edges uniformly, activate each edge with probability 1/2, and multiply the activated transpositions in their induced order. Its class law has a closed cycle-product formula, its cycle count is exactly shifted binomial, and its distribution is an integral convex mixture of conjugacy-averaged uniform walks on Young subgroups. The last statement turns the paper’s Young permutation character from a formal existence result into an equality between two random-permutation mechanisms.

1.3. Generating-set geometry and conventions The prefix recursion resembles a basis recursion, but rank-sized reflection generating sets are not generally the bases of a matroid. In I2(6), label the six reflection axes cyclically. The pairs {0, 1} and {3, 4} generate, whereas neither {1, 3} nor {1, 4} generates; basis exchange fails. We use only the conjugation-stable hypergraph of actual generating sets and its blocker. No matroid or Chow-ring theorem is invoked. The word “ordered” is essential. Literature notation RGS(W) often denotes an unordered set of reflections [15]; our RGSord(W) contains all r! orders of every rank-r set. In the complex case the full cyclic projector o(t)−1 ∑︁ j<o(t) tj must be used; replacing it by (1 + t)/2 is valid only for reflections of order two. Four positivity notions should not be conflated. Positivity of the coefficients of a group-algebra element, positivity of its represented operator, Schur positivity of a Frobenius characteristic, and nonnegative integral expansion in the h-basis are distinct statements. Here the first comes from probability normalization, the second from prefix recursion, the third follows from the second in type A, and the fourth requires the separate Abel and orbit arguments. The permutation representation is explicit in the Young-coset sense: it is a disjoint union of Young coset spaces once the integers cµ are known. We do not claim a canonical term-by-term bijection from activated ordered-tree objects to those cosets. The computational supplement gives exact regression certificates for normalizations and finite examples; all general-rank claims are proved in the text.

Remark 2.5 (Relation to parabolic-subset results). For a finite complex reflection group of rank r that can be generated by r reflections, Taylor [14] proves the stronger statement that every subset of any rank-sized reflection generating set generates a parabolic subgroup. Proposition 2.6 (Codimension-one prefixes are precisely parabolic). Let W be finite and well-generated of rank r. The subgroups generated by prefixes of length r −1 of tuples in RGSord(W) are exactly the parabolic subgroups of W of rank r −1.

A relative generating set in the rank-r group W therefore has cardinality r −(r −1) = 1. Thus it consists of a single reflection t, and hence ⟨P, t⟩= W. ## 9. Consequences and open problems

The paper produces two complementary structures. For every wellgenerated complex reflection group, the prefix identity turns a sum of generally non-self-adjoint projector words into a central positive-spectrum random walk. In type A, the same walk admits two exact samplers: one from activated edge-ordered trees and one from a convex mixture of Young-subgroup walks. This section records the computational and probabilistic consequences and formulates the missing combinatorics precisely.

9.1. Prefix computation and kernel certification Suppose a finite well-generated complex reflection group is given together with its reflections, the rank-(r −1) parabolic subgroups in Pr−1(W), and the completion sets C(K, W). Then (17) is a bottom-up dynamic program. Starting in rank zero, one computes AK,W and reuses the already constructed ΘK to assemble ΘW. In a chosen unitary representation one may work with the representation matrices directly instead of the full regular representation. Centrality reduces the final answer to irreducible scalars, and positivity provides an implementation check: a negative eigenvalue certifies a normalization or enumeration error. The recursion is not asserted to be polynomial time. Enumerating prefix subgroups and completion sets may be as difficult as enumerating the original generating sets. Its advantage is structural and auditable: every summand has a named subgroup, the ordered multiplicities are explicit, and (97) certifies the nullspace one positive summand at a time. The family calculation in Theorem 8.3 shows that this structure can collapse to a small collection of subgroup idempotents and thereby determine all convolution powers. The probabilistic normalization in Corollary 3.6 also rules out negative or oscillatory spectral modes. This places the construction in the representationtheoretic tradition of random walks on finite groups [1], but with a positivity mechanism adapted to ordered reflection generators rather than to a prescribed class measure.

9.3. Open problems

1. Natural coupling and species. Construct a canonical Sk-equivariant, product-preserving bijection between T • k and Y• k, or directly construct a tree, rooted-forest, parking, or factorization species whose fixed-point character is ak. The rooted-forest action of Can [25], the Abel forest interpretation of Sagan [21], and Prüfer-type encodings are concrete starting points. An unsigned refinement of the colored-cycle orbit argument would unify the presently separate positivity and integrality mechanisms.

2. Cutoff window and profile. Theorem 6.16 determines the leading totalvariation scale log k/(log 2 + 1/2) but not the cutoff window or limiting profile. If Xn ∼µ∗n k , then

E[# Fix(Xn)] = 1 + (k −1)λn (k−1,1),

and the proof of the cutoff lower bound shows that untouched vertices form a coupon-collector-like obstruction. Recent finite-level character asymptotics for conjugacy-invariant walks [34] suggest a route to a Poissonian profile, but the present increment is a class mixture rather than a single conjugacy class. Determine the O(1) window, the totalvariation and separation profiles, and whether a direct coupling realizes the same limiting obstruction.

3. Kernel classification. Determine the irreducible kernel of ΘW for every irreducible well-generated complex reflection group. The blocker recursion is an exact test, but the B3 example shows that no determinant-only rule can suffice.

4. Further uniform spectral families. Extend Theorem 8.3 to other infinite reflection families and express the positive irreducible scalars in terms of

degrees, codegrees, parabolic data, or reflection-Hurwitz invariants. Even a formula for the smallest positive scalar would sharpen the qualitative theorem.

5. Natural positive factorization. Find a combinatorial, arrangementtheoretic, or parabolic-incidence factorization ΘW = A∗A (or a comparably explicit sum of Hermitian squares) that proves positivity directly. The abstract square root exists by Theorem 3.4; the open problem is to explain it naturally from reflection-generating data, as occurs for neighboring shuffling operators.

6. Weighted, cyclotomic, and Hecke deformations. Find weights or deformations of the cyclic projectors for which the prefix completion operator still commutes with the prefix symmetrizer. Cyclotomic shuffle elements [13] and the braid/Hecke framework of Broué et al. [10] are natural comparison points, but formal parameter substitution alone does not preserve the commuting-positive factorization.

7. Beyond well-generated groups and efficient computation. Determine whether a variable-length or minimal-cardinality analogue exists when reflection rank exceeds the essential dimension. In parallel, identify families in which the prefix dynamic program avoids enumeration of all ordered good generating sets and prove output-sensitive complexity bounds.

The standalone supplement reconstructs the finite examples, the G(m, 1, 2) family certificates, and the type-A mixture and dominance-spectrum diagnostics. These checks support the normalizations and make the examples reproducible; the open problems concern new structural explanations, cutoff profiles, and all-rank extensions rather than larger finite tables.

### 2.3. What completeness does and does not say

For every fixed experiment pair in this class, the whole hierarchy is complete. It follows that there is no fixed-

object paradox: if all finite mixed-array laws are known exactly, the common alignment and the deficiency are

identified.

The theorem gives no uniform modulus translating a finite sample size into an error in deficiency. The

distinction is the same one that separates identifiability from estimability in graph-limit theory, where finite

sampled substructures and testing are tied to the cut topology [6]. A sequence may require larger and larger

samples before the finite hierarchy reaches the microscopic orbit carrying its decision value. The next section

constructs an exact family with this behavior.

Zucal’s right-convergence theorem [8] supplies a useful interpretation but not the load-bearing three-sort

proof: for probability-graphons, marked cut convergence is equivalent to convergence of quotient sets and

overlay/right observables. Therefore any counterexample that converges in our posterior-graphon cut topology

is invisible not only to fixed subgraph samples but to that entire family of dense global observables.

## 6. CONSEQUENCES, INTERFACES, AND EXACT SCOPE

The results separate three questions that are often conflated. Deficiency is a property of relatively aligned

experiments; posterior-array sampling is an acquisition model for that alignment; and an active oracle specifies

which relations may be requested. Relational order fixes the first possible collision arity, while the distinguishing

clutter records which coordinate sets actually matter and therefore determines the exact finite acquisition law.

In the linear-code witness, a syndrome distance fixes relational order and a dual-slice distance fixes the decision

gap; random nested pairs make simultaneous linear distances abundant over an alphabet fixed as code length

grows, and Reed–Solomon/MDS matrices attain the sharp frontier. In the permutation witness, harmonic

spectral geometry fixes the decision gap. In both cases Rényi block geometry fixes acquisition, while the oracle

interface fixes the third resource.

### 6.3. Recovery after controlling relational entropy

The recovery theorems in Section 5 supply the positive counterpart. They require a declared common-cell

structure with small paired diameter and statistical separation. The discovery-validation procedure does not

infer unseen rare cells individually. It aggregates their validation mass into a single missing coordinate and

propagates that uncertainty through a subprobability LP. Thus a returned interval certifies the observed

posterior-array model under its assumptions; it does not automatically learn a deployable raw-observation

channel.

Once a finite-dimensional or metric-entropy model is fixed, empirical-measure inequalities can improve

row-law terms [12]. They cannot by themselves overcome a missing common-label collision. The two sample

resources should therefore be tuned separately: columns discover relations, whereas rows resolve the values

attached to those relations.

### 6.4. Protected-state audit contract and falsifiability

The main article defines the exact protected-state release AR,S,t(Q, P): a curator draws an iid prior panel,

assigns persistent opaque handles, evaluates both experiments on the same hidden states, and releases posterior-

to-prior ratios without allowing the auditor to choose a future state by name. Private benchmarking and

privacy-preserving audit systems motivate the confidentiality constraint, but the theorem applies only when

the actual release satisfies this contract [17, 18, 19]. Any deployment or empirical implementation should

therefore report the following diagnostics.

1. Release and handles: specify the prior, verify that head and target entries bearing one handle refer

to the same sampled state, and document every quantization, compression, or added randomization as a

post-processing of the exact table.

5. Decision-theoretic closure: accompany a numerical deficiency claim with a simulator, a bounded-task

Conversely, revealing anchor identities or permitting addressable state queries changes the identified set and

can invalidate the anonymous-panel lower bound; such changes should be treated as design interventions rather

than protocol details.

### 6.5. Conclusion

Blackwell deficiency is stable once paired posterior geometry is aligned but can be only partially identified

when two experiments are known up to separate state relabelings. Every finite gap has an exact bounded-

task dual witness, yet protected posterior arrays acquire relative alignment only through shared columns. The

distinguishing-clutter theorem turns this correspondence problem into an exact finite acquisition law: relational

order fixes the first possible arity and the clutter fixes which relations actually distinguish. For the code witness,

dual first relative generalized Hamming weights determine relational order and the exact prior-average gap,

and support-minimal syndrome representatives form the clutter. Random nested pairs show that a high-order,

high-gap regime is abundant over an alphabet fixed with code length, while MDS matrices attain the exact

finite frontier and let both the gap and acquisition exponent approach one. For the permutation witness,

every (k −1)-subset is distinguishing and the decision gap is the harmonic quantity ∆(v). The exact finite

collision laws, quantitative Poisson approximations, minimax curves, and opaque-entry adaptive firewall make

these separations operational. Conditional recovery succeeds only after relational complexity is controlled. The

central methodological lesson is therefore not that more scalar samples always recover information order, but

that the sampling and oracle interfaces must expose the relation on which the order depends.

# A Twelve-Ray Fractional-Edge Process in a Convex Unitary Ensemble

Surya Tallavarjula1,a and Seyed Ali Rastegar2,b

1Department of Physics, University of California, Berkeley, Berkeley, CA 94720, USA; asurya_talla@berkeley.edu 2Department of Mathematics, University of California, Berkeley, Berkeley, CA 94720, USA; brastegar@berkeley.edu

Abstract. We construct an explicit globally strongly convex unitary ensemble whose equilibrium density vanishes as x1/3 at its left endpoint and as (1 −x)1/2 at its right endpoint. A degree perturbation n −N = O(N 3/8) extends the single equilibrium band through the fractional point on the N −3/4 left scale, while the remote soft edge moves on the N −5/8 scale. After centering the coupled endpoint flow, a cubic pullback of the Fokas–Its–Kitaev problem yields a determinant-one 2 × 2 local Riemann–Hilbert problem on a twelve-ray collision contour with three colliding quarter-root vertices. The cubic genealogy selects an exact C3-equivariant class. We prove unique solvability in that class for compact nonnegative deformation parameters by a folded half-positive identity and an entirefunction indicator argument, and establish a collision-uniform Beals–Coifman inverse on the invariant trace space. We then embed the model into a shrinking-disk RH/¯∂steepest-descent analysis using an explicit phase decomposition, weighted Cauchy moments, and exact circle matching. The rescaled correlation kernel converges locally, including its diagonal away from the STAR vertices. Uniform diagonal bounds and trace tightness yield trace-norm convergence on bounded windows. The limiting positive contraction therefore defines a determinantal point process, and the bounded-window point-process laws, joint count laws, Fredholm generating functions, and gap probabilities converge. At criticality, K0(X,X) = c0X1/3 + O(X−1), so the expected count is (3c0/4)L4/3 + O(log L); every fixed strict thinning has Fredholm cost Θ(L4/3).

MSC2020 subject classifications: Primary 60B20; secondary 60G55; 30E25; 47B10 Keywords: Random matrices; Unitary ensembles; Riemann–Hilbert problems; Determinantal point processes; Fractional edges; Trace-norm convergence

Electronic Supplementary Material. Online Resource 1 contains Appendices C–H, which give the detailed proofs of the collision-uniform inverse, canonical cubic expansion, registered local estimates, cubic-moment closure, global RH/¯∂trace-norm transfer, and quantitative coupled Abel inversion for the endpoint clocks. The main article retains all definitions, theorem statements, proof architecture, and the exact physical genealogy.

## 1. Introduction

At a regular endpoint of a unitary ensemble, the equilibrium density vanishes as a square root, the integrated action has exponent 3/2, and the N −2/3 scale leads to the Airy kernel [14, 28]. Other mechanisms produce other local laws: a soft edge may meet a fixed hard wall [9], a singularity may enter a regular edge layer [5, 20], a cut may be born with a finite population [3, 8], or an analytic density may be tuned through a higher polynomial criticality [10–12]. Interior cube-root cusps lead to Pearcey- or Boussinesq-type vector problems [4, 17, 29, 30]. A particularly close one-sided comparison is the recent hard-to-soft transition of Wang and Xu for Muttalib–Borodin ensembles: at the θ = 2 transition point the

This paper treats a different geometry. We construct an explicit scalar, globally strongly convex unitary ensemble whose equilibrium density satisfies

Adding O(N 3/8) particles occupies a new left segment of the same connected support on the N −3/4 scale. Thus the mechanism is growth of one band through a nonanalytic point, not the birth of a separate cut. The remote regular edge moves on the larger N −5/8 scale, but that motion enters the centered left phase only as a common analytic connection. The exact cubic pullback of the physical 2 × 2 Fokas–Its–Kitaev problem [15] produces a post-lens graph with a twelve-ray collision skeleton and three colliding quarter-root vertices. The exponent 1/3 alone is not the novelty claim. Real-exponent one-matrix models were already constructed by Janik and by Akemann–Vernizzi [1, 21]; cube-root densities also occur at two-sided interior cusps, and the Wang–Xu transition above realizes the same one-sided exponent in a vector biorthogonal setting. The conjunction proved here is narrower and structurally different: an explicit globally strongly convex scalar ensemble, a degree-driven two-endpoint clock, a physical 2 × 2 cubic quotient with a twelve-ray collision skeleton, a collision-uniform local inverse, and trace-norm convergence to the resulting determinantal process. The associated forbidden-gap problem and differential-algebraic classification lie beyond the scope of this article and are neither stated nor used here.

1.1. Proof architecture

The proof has two independent upstream branches which meet in the finite-N comparison:

equilibrium −→endpoint clocks −→registered phase packet,

exact C3 data −→equivariant moment cancellation −→folded vanishing

−→restricted index zero and STAR inverse,

(phase packet, STAR inverse) −→cubic matching −→global reconstruction

−→vertex mass −→trace norm and DPP laws.

Sections 2–3 establish the explicit equilibrium and state the coupled endpoint clocks; Online Resource 1, Appendix H, gives the complete quantitative perturbed-Abel proof, including both endpoint derivatives. Section 4 fixes the ray, branch, orientation, jump, and exact C3-equivariance conventions. Section 5 first upgrades weak homogeneous decay by invariant Cauchy-moment cancellation and then proves the all-parameter equivariant vanishing theorem by folding to a real-line problem, using a half-positive Hermitian identity, gluing the surviving rows to an entire scalar, and applying the criticalangle indicator inequality of Levin [23]. The raw operator is restricted to the invariant trace subspace; nilpotent residual weights give index zero there by a direct homotopy, and compact cross-chart terms preserve the index. The equivariant raw two-chart inverse and canonical cubic expansion are summarized there and proved in Online Resource 1, Appendices C and D. Section 6 compares the exact finite-N phase with the canonical phase on the expanding STAR window, closes the weighted coefficient moments, and performs the exact circle dressing. The technical estimates are proved in Online Resource 1, Appendices E and F. Sections 7–8 transport the result to the physical kernel, prove a collision-uniform diagonal bound with an identity-jump probe curve, and upgrade to trace-norm convergence. Online Resource 1, Appendix G, contains the full RH/¯∂and trace-tightness closure; Appendix H closes the independent endpoint-flow branch used by the phase packet.

1.2. Why trace norm is essential

Pointwise convergence away from a collision does not rule out a finite amount of diagonal mass concentrating in shrinking vertex neighborhoods. Such hidden mass changes traces and hence particle counts and Fredholm determinants. The proof therefore separates off-vertex Hilbert–Schmidt convergence from a uniform physical diagonal estimate at the vertices. Positivity then controls the off-diagonal trace-class blocks, and Gruemm’s theorem [16, 26] yields trace-norm convergence.

1.3. Scope

The theorem is restricted to the explicit potential constructed below and to compact nonnegative mass-flow intervals. The fractional criticality is deliberately engineered by placing the nonanalyticity of V∗at the unit-mass endpoint; the result is an explicit model theorem, not a stability or universality theorem. We do not prove universality for a general class of onesided cube-root edges, estimates uniform on the full half-line τ ≥0, the undeformed thinning-one large-hole asymptotic, or recurrence-coefficient asymptotics in the mixed left/right scaling. Online Resource 1 contains the long technical proofs supporting the endpoint-flow argument and Sections 5–8. No numerical computation enters the analytic proof.

# Forbidden Gaps at a One-Sided Fractional Edge:

# Two-Cut Equilibrium and Exact Pressure

Surya Tallavarjula1 and Seyed Ali Rastegar2

1Department of Physics, University of California, Berkeley, Berkeley, CA 94720, USA surya_talla@berkeley.edu ORCID: 0009-0007-7360-3514

2Department of Mathematics, University of California, Berkeley, Berkeley, CA 94720, USA rastegar@berkeley.edu ORCID: 0009-0001-5983-0469

Corresponding author: Surya Tallavarjula, surya_talla@berkeley.edu

## Abstract

For an explicit globally strongly convex unitary ensemble whose critical equilibrium density vanishes as x1/3 at its left endpoint, we study the constrained equilibrium obtained by forbidding particles in (0, a) while leaving x < 0 available. The minimizer develops two cuts, [c(a), 0] ∪[a, b(a)], with c(a) = −κ∗a + O(a5/3) and b(a) = 1 + Dgapa11/6 + O(a5/2). We prove the exact leading energy law Igap(a) −I∗= Cgapa8/3 + o(a8/3), identify Cgap from the limiting two-cut period problem, and recover the same coefficient independently from a moving-hard-edge pressure identity. A companion preprint supplies the boundedwindow twelve-ray determinantal kernel and its trace-norm finite-N limit. Using only those imported bounded-window facts, we prove finite-window strict contraction, strict-thinning diagonal exhaustion, and an undeformed integrable-kernel endpoint identity. The same period condition that selects κ∗is then shown to equalize the two scalar band constants in the associated large-parameter modulation problem. All deterministic equilibrium and pressure results are self-contained and do not depend on the companion preprint. The one-sided hard-wall benchmark is also sharpened to exact moment identities, separating its coefficient from the two-cut value. The final undeformed large-hole asymptotic is not claimed: it is reduced to either a finite-N moderate-deviation theorem or completion of the matrix-valued steepest-descent analysis.

Keywords: Unitary ensembles; logarithmic potential theory; determinantal point processes; fractional edges; Riemann–Hilbert problems; large gaps

## 1 Introduction

Large-gap probabilities in unitary random-matrix limits are collective objects: the leading exponential cost reflects a rearrangement of the equilibrium measure, while the limiting Fredholm determinant encodes the microscopic process. Classical undeformed large-gap asymptotics include the sine- and Airy-kernel problems and the determination of their constant terms [1–3]. A complementary body of work studies thinning or varying external potentials and the transition toward the undeformed endpoint, including the bulk sine process, conditioned or thinned circular ensembles, and incomplete spectra [4–8]. Airy determinants with discontinuities provide a softedge counterpart [9]. Multi-interval problems can introduce genuinely higher-genus geometry, as in two large sine-kernel intervals and multi-interval Bessel gaps [10, 11]. These works make clear that the distinction between strict thinning and the undeformed endpoint is established methodology rather than a novelty claim of the present paper. The problem considered here has a different geometric source. We construct explicitly a globally strongly convex scalar potential V∗whose unit-mass equilibrium density is

ρ1(x) = c0x1/3(1 −x)1/21[0,1](x).

The exponent 1/3 by itself is not new: nonpolynomial real-exponent matrix models and other singular-edge mechanisms are known [12,13], and recent critical-edge work treats different powers

### 1.3 Relation to existing large-gap and critical-edge work

The novelty claim is therefore narrower than “critical-edge large gaps” or the distinction between strict thinning and the undeformed endpoint. The latter has a substantial literature: the sine process in a varying potential is analyzed uniformly through thinning regimes in [4–6]; conditioning and thinning of the circular unitary ensemble (CUE) are treated in [7]; incomplete soft-, hard-, and bulk-edge spectra are treated through an extended Jimbo–Miwa–Ueno differential in [8]; and Airy determinants with discontinuities are treated in [9]. The classical undeformed Airy and bulk constants remain basic reference points [1,2].

3


<!-- Page 4 -->


Nor is two-component geometry itself new. Two large sine-kernel intervals and multi-interval Bessel gaps require higher-genus scalar constructions [10, 11]. Birth-of-a-cut transitions under parameter tuning are analyzed in [17–19]. Polynomial higher-critical and soft/hard collision mechanisms lead to other local models [20–24]. A particularly close one-sided comparison is the Muttalib–Borodin hard-to-soft transition of Wang and Xu [25]: at θ = 2 a 1/3 critical vanishing also appears, but in a biorthogonal setting with a 3×3 vector Riemann–Hilbert problem. On the large-gap side, Claeys, Girotti, and Stivigny obtained hard-edge Muttalib–Borodin asymptotics [35], subsequently sharpened to higher-order asymptotics and explicit multiplicative constants by Charlier, Lenells, and Mauersberger [36]. Cafasso and Pinheiro recently studied multiplicative statistics at a different 5/2 critical edge and their KdV structure [14]. What is new here is the conjunction of a gap-induced newborn negative cut at a one-sided fractional edge, the coupled a and a11/6 endpoint clocks, an exact pressure coefficient for that constrained geometry, and the identification of the equilibrium period root with the scalar bandmatching parameter of the companion twelve-ray IIKS problem. The model is explicit rather than universal; no general-potential universality theorem is claimed.

Remark 9.18 (What diagonal exhaustion closes). Theorem 9.11 gives an unconditional growingwindow transfer for every fixed strict thinning, uniformly on compact subintervals of [0, 1). Corollary 9.12 gives the equivalent cofinal-pair formulation. Neither statement supplies a rate or controls a predetermined growing sequence. Proposition 9.14 identifies the stronger relative topology required for a quantitative same-sequence comparison at γ = 1. In contrast, Proposition 9.3 and Theorem 9.17 show that coefficient identification itself can be transferred diagonally: once a right-cofinal finite-N shrinking-gap moderate-deviation theorem is proved, fixed-window trace-norm convergence is enough. The probability-level moderate-deviation law is therefore the sole remaining input on this route.

Remark 9.19 (Why γ = 1 is different). For strict thinning, elementary spectral bounds control the Fredholm cost by the mean count, but those bounds degenerate at γ = 1. The L4/3 meancount scale should therefore not be confused with the stronger collective cost of an undeformed hole.

The support theorem makes the finite-a equilibrium coefficient unconditional, while Proposition 8.1 gives its exact pressure/quadrature representation. Corollary 8.2 transfers it to the deterministic shrinking-gap scale whenever LN = o(N3/4). Independently, Theorem 9.11 transfers every fixed strict thinning to a growing window chosen by diagonalization. No explicit rate or predetermined polynomial window is asserted. For a fixed macroscopic forbidden interval, the empirical-measure large-deviation principle identifies the constrained weighted-energy excess as the N 2 rate [38,39]. To conclude

On the direct limiting route, Theorem 9.4 and Proposition 9.5 formulate the γ = 1 problem as a large-parameter IIKS Riemann–Hilbert problem, and Corollary 9.9 shows that it is enough to prove the local endpoint law RL(L, L) ∼2PgapL5/3.
